# Conspiracy of Credit Part 1

First listed: 2026-05-13 | Evaluation cutoff: 2026-11-10

[Back to library](../README.md)

## Source versions

- [Substack: Conspiracy of Credit Part 1](https://realeismanplaybook.substack.com/p/conspiracy-of-credit-part-1) - 2026-05-13

Earliest listed publication among matched versions, not proof of an unedited contemporaneous archive. Claim timestamps refer to the reviewed version.

## Summary

Eisman places private credit in an early contraction phase, emphasizing redemption pressure, software concentration, bank links and life-insurer exposure. Blue Owl filings confirm striking tender demand, and supervisory evidence supports stronger bank capital. However, gross redemption requests do not equal forced asset sales or net outflows. Claims that virtually all post-2008 lending growth was private, all subprime mortgages were securitized, and rates fell in 2018 are overstated or wrong. The aggregate CDO multiplier and software exposure require tighter definitions. His smaller-than-2008 crisis thesis remains unresolved, with explicit insurer caveats.

The episode identifies meaningful liquidity and concentration vulnerabilities but blends supported examples with universal claims and stock-flow confusion. Preserve the cautious systemic comparison and separate a sector credit cycle from an economy-wide credit-led recession. Captions contain genuine incomplete sentences; no missing AI prediction is reconstructed.

## Material claims

<a id="substack-202888778-c001"></a>
### 001. There has been no credit cycle since the global financial crisis.

**Mixed** | Steve Eisman | explanation | major

[Source at 0:22-0:38](https://realeismanplaybook.substack.com/p/conspiracy-of-credit-part-1) | Stance: asserted | Horizon: not stated

The Fed documents a meaningful energy credit downturn in 2014-2016. His later narrower claim about a credit-led economy-wide recession is different.

Qualification: Later he says no credit-cycle-induced recession, which is narrower than the opening assertion.

Assessment test: Distinguish sector cycles, economy-wide credit contractions and recession causes.

- [2016 supervision and regulation annual report](https://www.federalreserve.gov/publications/2016-ar-supervision-and-regulation.htm) (2017): Energy-sector cash-flow deterioration and excessive debt produced a significant rise in defaults and bankruptcies after the commodity downturn, documenting a post-2008 sector credit cycle.

<a id="substack-202888778-c002"></a>
### 002. Almost all lending growth since 2008 has occurred in private credit rather than banks.

**Wrong** | Steve Eisman | explanation | major

[Source at 0:30-0:39](https://realeismanplaybook.substack.com/p/conspiracy-of-credit-part-1) | Stance: asserted | Horizon: not stated

Bank loans expanded by trillions between 2008 and 2026, exceeding the entire estimated private-credit market. The all-lending formulation is untenable.

Qualification: A claim about a narrower leveraged-buyout segment would require a separately stated denominator.

Assessment test: Compare consistent lending stocks and flows, including definition changes.

- [H.8 October 31 2008](https://www.federalreserve.gov/releases/h8/20081031/) (2008-10-31): All-commercial-bank loans and leases were roughly $7.3 trillion in the displayed latest weeks.
- [H.8 November 6 2026](https://www.federalreserve.gov/releases/h8/current/) (2026-11-06): All-commercial-bank loans and leases were about $14.2 trillion, materially above 2008. Definition changes limit exact historical growth calculations but do not erase the large expansion.
- [Private-credit vulnerabilities](https://www.fsb.org/2026/05/report-on-vulnerabilities-in-private-credit/) (2026-05-06): Private credit estimated at $1.5-2 trillion has grown with limited visibility and deepening insurer, bank and private-equity links; leverage and concentration are vulnerabilities.

<a id="substack-202888778-c003"></a>
### 003. Private-credit stress will produce losses and perhaps a recession, but likely less chaos than 2008 because banks are better capitalized.

**Unresolved** | Steve Eisman | forecast | major

[Source at 1:26-1:43](https://realeismanplaybook.substack.com/p/conspiracy-of-credit-part-1) | Stance: asserted | Horizon: not stated

Bank resilience has support, but neither the eventual cycle loss nor the claimed recession severity is settled by the cutoff.

Assessment test: Track realized losses, bank transmission and macro outcomes.

- [Banking system conditions](https://www.federalreserve.gov/publications/2025-december-supervision-and-regulation-report-banking-system-conditions.htm) (2025-12): More than 99% of banks were well capitalized and the 2025 large-bank stress test supported resilience under its specified severe scenario.
- [Private-credit vulnerabilities](https://www.fsb.org/2026/05/report-on-vulnerabilities-in-private-credit/) (2026-05-06): Private credit estimated at $1.5-2 trillion has grown with limited visibility and deepening insurer, bank and private-equity links; leverage and concentration are vulnerabilities.

<a id="substack-202888778-c006"></a>
### 006. Equity investors must monitor debt markets because senior financing problems can destroy residual equity value.

**Right** | Steve Eisman | analytical principle | major

[Source at 2:42-3:03](https://realeismanplaybook.substack.com/p/conspiracy-of-credit-part-1) | Stance: asserted | Horizon: not stated

This follows from equity's residual position in a simple capital structure.

Conditional reasoning: Let enterprise asset value be V and debt claim D. In the simple limited-liability case, equity payoff=max(V-D,0). Asset impairment or a financing failure can eliminate residual value even while creditors recover part of their claim.

Assessment test: Inspect issuer-specific priority, guarantees and refinancing needs.

### 038. Previously diverse exposures may become highly correlated, with standard deviation approaching one.

**Mixed** | Steve Eisman | explanation | major

[Source at 15:58-16:21](https://realeismanplaybook.substack.com/p/conspiracy-of-credit-part-1) | Stance: asserted | Horizon: not stated

The common-exposure warning is valid, but standard deviation is not correlation and approaching one has no universal diversification meaning.

Conditional reasoning: Correlation is covariance divided by the product of standard deviations and ranges from -1 to 1. Standard deviation changes with units: multiplying returns by 100 multiplies it by 100 without changing correlation. Thus standard deviation approaching 1 cannot establish near-perfect correlation.

Assessment test: Estimate covariance and correlation rather than using a unit-dependent volatility threshold.

## Framework and tools

- Separate sector credit cycles from recession causes.
- Measure net outflows and liquidity resources alongside gross tender requests.
- Trace bank financing of ostensibly nonbank credit.
- Compare common borrower exposures rather than labels.
- Use consistent stocks, flows, notionals and net losses.
- Stress insurer liabilities and assets together.
- Treat ratings as opinions and test shared assumptions independently.

Tools and charts discussed, not a complete visual inspection:

- Four-stage credit-cycle framework
- BDC debt/equity and asset coverage
- Blue Owl OCIC and OTIC tender requests and caps
- Bank loans and unused commitments
- Subprime originations and CDO exposure comparison
- Software sector classifications and subscription revenues
- Life-insurer duration and offshore reinsurance
